0.note: The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]

1.note: Here the speaker is using one part, the **heart**, to represent the whole person. If another body part represents this in your culture, you could use it or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with all my being] or [with my whole person]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wonders**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [all the marvelous things you do] or [all your marvelous actions]

2.note: The two words **rejoice** and **exult** may express a single idea. The word **exult** tells how the psalmist is rejoicing. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [I will rejoice exuberantly]

Here, his **name** represents Yahweh: him, his reputation, and what he does. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I will sing praise to you]

3.note: The last part of verse 3 (**from your face**) and the first line of verse 4 give the reason why the **enemies turn back, they stumble and perish**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is the reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [because of your angry presence, and because]

Here, **face** represents the presence of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in your presence]

4.note: Alternate translation: [you have ruled on] or [you have declared] or [you have accomplished]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **justice**, **claim**, and **righteousness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [For you have answered me justly when I petitioned in your court … a righteous judge]

The two words **justice** and **claim** may express a single idea. The word **justice** tells how Yahweh views the author’s legal **claim**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [you have ruled that my claim is just] or [you have answered my just claim]

Here, **throne** represents kingship. Kings had authority to judge people, and they would sit on their throne when they judged. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you are like a king who judged his people from his throne] or [you are a king]
Alternate translation: [you are like a royal judge who always issues correct judgments from his throne] or [you sit on your judgment throne and judge righteously]

5.note: This could mean: (1) Yahweh caused these people to be forgotten. The end of verse 6 is parallel with this verse if you favor this interpretation. Alternate translation: [you have caused them to be forgotten as if their name was blotted out] or [no one will ever remember them again], (2) Yahweh will not give these people eternal life (other parts of the Bible speak of this as blotting them out from the Book of Life). Alternate translation: [you send them to eternal punishment]
See how you translated the phrase **the wicked** in 1:1.

The terms **forever** and **ever** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [eternally]

6.note: In this verse, the word **enemy** is singular in form, but it refers to all enemies as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form to make this clear. Alternate translation: [The enemies are finished]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **desolation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [they are made desolate forever] or [you make them desolate forever]

Here, **cities** is spoken of as if it were a plant that could be **pulled up**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when you destroyed their cities]

Here, **remembrance** is spoken of as if it were a living being that could die. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [All remembrance of them has stopped] or [There is no longer any remembrance of them]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **remembrance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [No one remembers them at all]

The psalmist uses the words **As for them** here to indicate an emphatic contrast between what happens to the **enemy** and Yahweh. In your translation, indicate this strong contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Now speaking of the enemy]

7.note: Here, to **sit** represents the authority of the king to judge. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [reigns] or [is king]

The phrase **his throne** represents God’s rule. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He rules in order to judge people] or [He rules over people justly]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **justice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to do justly]

8.q: וְ⁠ה֗וּא יִשְׁפֹּֽט־תֵּבֵ֥ל בְּ⁠צֶ֑דֶק יָדִ֥ין לְ֝אֻמִּ֗ים בְּ⁠מֵישָׁרִֽים
8.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. Translate them according to the decisions your team has made regarding translating parallelism in Hebrew poetry. See the Introduction to Psalms for more information. Alternate translation: [as for him, he will judge the world with righteousness, yes, he will adjudicate for the peoples with fairness] or [as for him, he will judge the people of the world with righteousness and fairness]

Here, **the world** refers to all the people in the world. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [everyone in the world]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **righteousness** and **fairness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [righteously … fairly]

9.q: וִ֘⁠יהִ֤י יְהוָ֣ה מִשְׂגָּ֣ב לַ⁠דָּ֑ךְ מִ֝שְׂגָּ֗ב לְ⁠עִתּ֥וֹת בַּצָּרָֽה
9.note: Here the psalmist is speaking of **Yahweh** as if he were a place that people could go to for safety. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And may Yahweh protect the oppressed, may he protect them in times with distress] or [And may Yahweh provide safety for those who are oppressed, making them safe in times with distress]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **distress**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for distressing times]

10.note: Here, **your name** represents Yahweh and his reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those who know you] or [those who have heard what you do]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **knowers** and **seekers**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [people who know … people who seek you]

11.note: Here, being **the sitter** represents sitting on the throne as king. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the king] or [the ruler]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **praises**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Praise Yahweh with a song] or [Sing to praise Yahweh]

12.note: Here, **the seeker** refers to the avenger of blood, who hunts down and kills a murderer. Yahweh is the avenger in this case. See Numbers 35 for more information.

The implication is that the **seeker of vengeance** will remember to avenge for the murder of **them** (the victims calling for justice). You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [remembered to avenge those who were murdered]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **seeker**, **vengeance**, and **bloodshed**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [the one who seeks to avenge anyone who was murdered … them]

If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this double negative that consists of the negative particle **not** and the negative idea of **forget**. Alternate translation: [he surely remembers]

The psalmist is using the adjective **poor** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [poor people]

13.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **mercy**, **affliction**, and **haters**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [Be merciful to me … how I am afflicted by those who hate me]
The implication is that Yahweh will act, not just **See**. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Take action because of]

Here, **death** is spoken of as if it were a city that had **gates** through which people enter in. If someone is near the **gates of death**, it means that he will die soon. Keeping someone from dying is spoken of as lifting him away from the gates of death. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [O you who can rescue me from death] or [O you who can keep me from dying]

14.note: The **gate** is the place of trade, business, and justice in the ancient city. If your readers would not be familiar with this, you could use the location where similar things happen in your area, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [in the central market of] or [in the place of trade and settling legal disputes of]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **praise** and **salvation**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [your praiseworthy deeds … because you saved me] or [the reasons to praise you … because you are a savior]

15.q: נ֤וֹדַ֨ע ׀ יְהוָה֮ מִשְׁפָּ֪ט עָ֫שָׂ֥ה & נוֹקֵ֣שׁ רָשָׁ֑ע
15.note: Both the cause and the result of everything else in verses 15–16 are in the sentence **Yahweh has revealed himself, he has done justice**. The cause of the wicked nations being trapped by their own traps is Yahweh doing justice; the result is that he is revealed as being just. In your translation, use a structure that makes these connections clear. Alternate translation: [This happens because Yahweh is acting justly toward them. Yahweh reveals himself by justly causing the wicked to be ensnared]

15.q: טָבְע֣וּ ג֭וֹיִם בְּ⁠שַׁ֣חַת עָשׂ֑וּ בְּ⁠רֶֽשֶׁת־ז֥וּ טָ֝מָ֗נוּ נִלְכְּדָ֥ה רַגְלָֽ⁠ם
15.note: People dig pits so they can catch animals that fall into them. They also hide nets to catch animals. Here digging a **pit** or hiding a **net** represents making plans to destroy people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The nations are like people who dig a pit for others and then fall into it; like people who hide a net to catch people and then get caught in it] or [The nations get caught in their own traps.]

15.q: טָבְע֣וּ ג֭וֹיִם בְּ⁠שַׁ֣חַת עָשׂ֑וּ בְּ⁠רֶֽשֶׁת־ז֥וּ טָ֝מָ֗נוּ נִלְכְּדָ֥ה רַגְלָֽ⁠ם
15.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. Translate them according to the decisions your team has made regarding translating parallelism in Hebrew poetry. See the Introduction to Psalms for more information.

16.note: The word **himself** indicates that the object of the verb is the same as the subject of the verb. Use a way that is natural in your language to indicate that the same person fills two roles in the sentence. Alternate translation: [has revealed Yahweh]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **justice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [things justly]
See how you translated the phrase **the wicked** in 1:1.

The expression **the wicked is ensnared** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the wicked person harms himself by the wicked things he does]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **work**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [by what he does] or [by his own evil deeds]

17.note: Verses 17–18 form a poetic device called a chiasm where the inner two lines parallel each other and the outer two lines also parallel each other. In this case this artistic device creates a strong contrast between the verses by contrasting people forgetting God with God not forgetting the needy and contrasts the death of the wicked with the hope of the afflicted which does not die. If your language has a poetic structure that can make contrasts stand out markedly like this, consider using it here.
See how you translated the idea of “turn back” in verse 3, as this is likely connected.

Here, **are forgetful of God** is a common expression that means “they forget or ignore God.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use an expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [dismiss God] or [neglect to honor and worship God]

If the connection between **all nations** in this phrase and the **wicked** of the last phrase is not clear, you may want to show this connection. Alternate translation: [the wicked ones from all nations who are forgetful of God]

Here, **nations** represents the people in the nations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [people in every nation]

18.note: The expression **the needy will not be forgotten** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [God will not always forget the needy]

The figure of speech here expresses a strongly positive meaning by using a negative word, **not**, together with an expression that is the opposite of the intended meaning. If it would be helpful in your language, you could emphasize the positive meaning. Alternate translation: [the needy will be remembered eventually]

The negation in the first clause of this verse carries over to the second half. Translate this in a way that both halves of the verse are negated (but making a positive statement as the previous note explains). Alternate translation: [indeed, the hope of the afflicted will not perish forever] or [neither will the hope of the afflicted perish forever] or (assuming the first half is translated positively) [the hope of the afflicted lives on]

Here, **hope** is spoken of as if it were something that could perish. This would mean that what they hope for does not happen. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [nor will the oppressed hope forever without results] or [someday what the afflicted hope for will happen]

19.note: Here, **Arise** represents starting to act. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Take action]

Here judging includes punishing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [let nations be judged and punished]

Here, **on your face** represents being in Yahweh’s presence, which can be considered in his courtroom (as in the UST). If it would be helpful, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [In your presence]

The expression **let nations be judged** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Judge the nations in your presence] or [Take the nations into your presence and punish them]

20.note: Here, **terror** is spoken of as something that could be **put** to the wicked, meaning to cause them to feel terror. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Make them be terrified Yahweh!] or [Terrify them Yahweh!]

Here the psalmist is speaking of **nations** as if they were living humans. There are two points: (1) nations do not last forever; they pass away or are mortal like humans, and (2) the leaders of nations are not gods, but humans who die. In both instances, they need to recognize that Yahweh is the supreme, never-ending power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May nations know they are temporary] or [May wicked human kings stop pretending to be eternal gods]
